sections.title: The mountain nobody stands on
sections.intro_md:
On 25 May 1955 two British climbers, Joe Brown and George Band, reached the top of the third highest mountain on Earth, and then did not step onto it. They stopped a few metres short of the summit of Kangchenjunga because their expedition had promised the Chogyal, the king of Sikkim, that the home of the land's guardian god would stay untrodden.

That is Sikkim in one scene. A state of about six lakh people, smaller than many Indian districts, where a mountain is a deity, monasteries forecast the year from a vase of water, and modern politics, an American queen, a 1975 referendum, a dam swept away by a glacial lake, all happen in sight of the same five snow peaks.

spotlights.name: Kangchenjunga, the mountain nobody stands on

where.label: Sikkim-Nepal border, seen from Pelling and Gangtok

spotlights.when: First climbed 25 May 1955, summit left untouched
spotlights.spot_it: A wall of five snow summits filling the north-west skyline from Gangtok or Pelling, turning pink at sunrise.
spotlights.story_md: At 8,586 m Kangchenjunga is the third highest mountain on Earth, and until 1852 surveyors thought it was the highest. Its Tibetan name means roughly 'five treasures of the great snow'. For Sikkim it is not a peak but a guardian deity. In 1955 a British team led by Charles Evans got two men, Joe Brown and George Band, to within a few metres of the top. They stopped short on purpose, keeping a promise made to the Chogyal of Sikkim that the summit would stay untrodden. Many climbers since have kept the same custom.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains Sikkim in one image: a state whose biggest landmark is treated as a god, not a trophy.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first men to climb it chose not to stand on it.

sections.title: Sikkim in eight numbers
sections.intro_md:
Sikkim is a thumb of land, about **116 km north to south and 65 km across**, wedged between Nepal to the west, Tibet (China) to the north and east, Bhutan to the south-east and West Bengal to the south. It covers **7,096 square km**: only Goa is smaller. Census 2011 counted **610,577** people, the fewest of any state, at 86 per square km.

It climbs from 280 m at the Teesta in the south to 8,586 m on Kangchenjunga, so it holds tropical valleys and glaciers within a day's drive. Gangtok is the capital. Since 2021 there are **six districts**: Gangtok, Mangan, Namchi, Gyalshing, Pakyong and Soreng. Sikkim became India's 22nd state on 16 May 1975, keeps special protections under Article 371F, and old Sikkimese residents pay no income tax on income from the state, a rule widened by the Supreme Court in 2023. It now ranks first among states in income per head.

sections.title: Snow, one river and five climates
sections.intro_md:
Sikkim is one long slope. In the north, above 4,000 m, is a cold desert of glaciers and lakes on the Tibetan plateau's edge, where Gurudongmar sits. Below that come alpine meadows and rhododendron forest, then oak and fir, then terraced farms and cardamom groves, and at the bottom, near Rangpo, the hot, humid Teesta valley at under 300 m. Almost all of it drains into one river, the Teesta.

This compression makes Sikkim one of the richest places for wildlife in India: about 550 bird species in the national park alone, dozens of rhododendrons, hundreds of orchids, red pandas and snow leopards. It also makes the state fragile. Steep slopes, heavy monsoon rain, earthquakes and growing glacial lakes mean landslides and floods are part of everyday life.

spotlights.name: The Teesta, Sikkim's one river

where.label: Teesta at Rangpo, Sikkim-West Bengal border

spotlights.when: Rises in North Sikkim, joins the Brahmaputra in Bangladesh
spotlights.spot_it: A fast green-grey river at the bottom of every deep valley, with the national highway clinging to the slope above it.
spotlights.story_md: Almost every stream in Sikkim ends up in one river. The Teesta begins in glacial lakes near the Tibetan border, falls more than 5,000 m through the state, takes in the Rangeet at Melli, and leaves for West Bengal and Bangladesh, where it joins the Brahmaputra. That fall is why Sikkim is lined with hydropower dams. It is also why floods here are so violent. In October 2023 a glacial lake far upstream burst and the Teesta wiped out a 1,200 MW dam, bridges and whole stretches of NH10 in one night.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The river is Sikkim's power supply, its highway corridor and its biggest hazard, all at once.
spotlights.memory_hook: One river drains a whole state, and once in a while it erases it.

spotlights.name: Gurudongmar Lake

where.label: North Sikkim, about 5 km from the Chinese border

spotlights.spot_it: A wide turquoise lake in a bare brown basin, snow peaks behind it and prayer flags whipping along the shore.
spotlights.story_md: Gurudongmar sits at more than 5,100 m (the state government says 5,430 m; maps say a little over 5,150 m), about 190 km from Gangtok and 5 km from China. It is fed by a glacier and helps form the source of the Teesta. Buddhists say Guru Padmasambhava touched part of it so that it would never freeze completely and herders could drink. In the late 1990s an army Sikh regiment built a gurdwara here, saying Guru Nanak had visited. Local protests followed, a state committee sided with the Buddhist claim, and in 2001 the building was handed to Lachen Monastery.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how sacred geography, the army and the border meet in North Sikkim.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lake so high that one blessed corner is the only part allowed to stay liquid.

spotlights.name: Tsomgo (Changu) Lake
spotlights.when: Frozen in winter, sometimes into May
spotlights.spot_it: An oval glacial lake at 3,753 m beside the Nathu La road, with decorated yaks for hire on the bank.
spotlights.story_md: Tsomgo is 40 km from Gangtok on the road to Nathu La, at 3,753 m. It is small, about 836 m long and up to 15 m deep, and it freezes in winter. The name is usually read as 'source of the lake'. Monks once read the future from its changing colours, and on Guru Purnima jhakri faith healers gather to use its water. Because it is inside a restricted border zone, every visitor needs a permit, and foreigners a special one. For most tourists it is the first high-altitude place they ever stand in.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most visited lake in Sikkim and the easiest taste of the high Himalaya.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lake you need a permit to look at.

spotlights.name: Khangchendzonga National Park
spotlights.spot_it: Glaciers, moraine and rhododendron forest climbing from 1,829 m to over 8,500 m, with Kangchenjunga at the top.
spotlights.story_md: The park covers about 1,784 square km, a quarter of Sikkim, and climbs from 1,829 m to the top of the world's third highest mountain. In July 2016 UNESCO made it India's first 'mixed' World Heritage Site, listed for both nature and culture. The culture part is the belief that this is a beyul, a hidden sacred land, and the home of the mountain god. The nature part is about 550 bird species and six kinds of wild cat, including the snow leopard and the clouded leopard, caught on camera traps.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is still the only Indian World Heritage Site listed equally for nature and for faith.
spotlights.memory_hook: India's first mixed heritage site: half of it counted in species, half in prayers.

spotlights.name: Red panda, the state animal
spotlights.spot_it: A cat-sized animal with rust-red fur, a white-masked face and a thick ringed tail, usually curled up high in a tree.
spotlights.story_md: The red panda was named a panda about 45 years before the giant panda was. It is not a bear and not a raccoon: it has a family of its own, Ailuridae. Like the giant panda it lives mostly on bamboo, which is poor food, so it sleeps a lot and keeps its metabolism low. It is listed as Endangered, threatened by forest loss and by being cut off into small patches. Sikkim made it the state animal, and it lives in the temperate forests of the Khangchendzonga park and the Singalila ridge on the Nepal border.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the mascot of the eastern Himalaya and an indicator of whether the forests are healthy.
spotlights.memory_hook: The original panda, and it is red.

spotlights.name: Rhododendrons of Yumthang
spotlights.spot_it: A wide valley floor at about 3,600 m with whole hillsides of red, pink, white and yellow blossoms on twisted trees.
spotlights.story_md: The rhododendron is Sikkim's state tree, and Yumthang Valley, about 150 km north of Gangtok, is where it shows off. The Shingba Rhododendron Sanctuary around it holds more than 24 species. Across the state the count runs to several dozen. From late February to June the slopes flower in sequence as spring climbs the mountain, low-altitude red first, high-altitude pale and dwarf species last. There is a hot spring in the valley, and yaks graze the meadows once the snow goes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: These flowers started a gardening craze in Victorian Britain and still draw Sikkim's spring tourists.
spotlights.memory_hook: Spring climbs Yumthang one colour at a time.

spotlights.name: Noble dendrobium, the state flower
spotlights.spot_it: Clusters of waxy white flowers tipped with purple, each with a dark maroon blotch in the throat, hanging off cane-like stems.
spotlights.story_md: Sikkim's state flower is the noble dendrobium, *Dendrobium nobile*, an orchid that grows on tree trunks and rocks in the foothill forests. It flowers in spring on bare, jointed canes. Sikkim counts several hundred orchid species, one of the highest densities in India for its size, and orchids are a quiet business: the government runs orchid sanctuaries and an orchidarium near Rumtek, and the President visited the orchidarium in May 2026. In Chinese medicine the same plant is sold as shi hu, which is why wild plants are poached.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Orchids are part of Sikkim's case that a small state can be one of India's biodiversity capitals.
spotlights.memory_hook: Purple-tipped, maroon-throated, growing on a tree that is not its own.

spotlights.name: Blood pheasant, the state bird
spotlights.spot_it: A plump grey bird with a red eye-ring and red streaks on the breast and tail, as if splashed with blood, scratching in snow.
spotlights.story_md: The blood pheasant gets its name from the male's crimson streaks on face, throat and breast. It lives higher than most pheasants, in fir and rhododendron forest close to the snowline, and moves up and down the slope with the seasons. Flocks are often seen walking on snow near the Nathu La road and in the Khangchendzonga park. It is not rare across its whole range, but in Sikkim it is a symbol of the cold forests that sit between the farmed valleys and the glaciers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the bird of the zone most tourists drive through on the way to the passes.
spotlights.memory_hook: A grey bird that looks like it lost a fight with a paint pot.

sections.title: Lepchas, lamas and kings
sections.intro_md:
The Lepcha were here first, farming, hunting and worshipping the mountains. From around the 14th century Bhutia clans came south from Tibet, and the two peoples are said to have sworn brotherhood with Kangchenjunga as witness. In 1642 three Tibetan lamas met at Yuksom and consecrated Phuntsog Namgyal as the first Chogyal. His dynasty ruled for 333 years.

It was rarely easy. Bhutan occupied parts of the kingdom from 1700 to 1706. The Gorkhas of Nepal overran it in 1788. The British, who returned land to Sikkim in 1817, then took Darjeeling in 1835, annexed more after a botanist's arrest in 1849, and made the kingdom a protectorate by the Treaty of Tumlong in 1861. The capital moved from Yuksom to Rabdentse, to Tumlong, and in 1894 to Gangtok.

spotlights.name: The Lepcha, Sikkim's first people
spotlights.spot_it: Men in a striped hand-woven dumprá wrapped like a cloak, a flat bamboo-and-cane hat, and a long knife at the waist.
spotlights.story_md: The Lepcha call themselves Rongkup, and their homeland Mayel Lyang. They are generally accepted as Sikkim's oldest people. About 80,000 live across Sikkim, Darjeeling, Kalimpong, Nepal and Bhutan. Their clans are named after sacred lakes and peaks, and in their belief people came from the snows of Kangchenjunga. They built stilted houses of wood and bamboo without nails, and they have their own script, developed in the 17th and 18th centuries. Many are now Buddhist or Christian, but the old Mun shamans still practise, often alongside lamas at the same ceremony.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Every later layer of Sikkim, Bhutia kings, Nepali farmers, Indian state, sits on top of the Lepcha one.
spotlights.memory_hook: People who say they were made from Kangchenjunga's snow.

spotlights.name: Yuksom and the Norbugang throne
spotlights.spot_it: A plain stone seat under a huge old cryptomeria tree, with a white chorten beside it, in a quiet village at 1,780 m.
spotlights.story_md: In 1642 three lamas coming from Tibet met at Yuksom and consecrated a local chief, Phuntsog Namgyal, as the first Chogyal, the 'righteous king'. The name Yuksom is said to mean 'meeting place of the three learned monks'. The stone seat used for the ceremony, the Norbugang throne, still stands. The Namgyal dynasty founded that day ruled for 333 years, until 1975. Today Yuksom is better known as the starting point of the trek to Dzongri and Goecha La, and Dubdi, said to be Sikkim's oldest monastery, founded in 1701, is an hour's walk up the hill.
spotlights.why_it_matters: This stone chair is where the kingdom of Sikkim began.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three lamas, one chair, 333 years of kings.

spotlights.name: Rabdentse ruins
spotlights.spot_it: Low grey stone walls and three chortens on a forest ridge, with Kangchenjunga filling the horizon behind them.
spotlights.story_md: In 1670 the second Chogyal moved his capital from Yuksom to this ridge near Pelling. Rabdentse was the seat of the kingdom for about 140 years, and its life was one long siege. Bhutanese forces occupied parts of Sikkim from 1700 to 1706. In 1788 the Gorkha army of Nepal captured it and sent the king into exile in Tibet. The capital moved again, to Tumlong and later Gangtok. What is left are walls, chortens and a stone throne for judges, now protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the evidence that Sikkim was squeezed by bigger neighbours long before the British or India arrived.
spotlights.memory_hook: A capital with the best view in the Himalaya and the worst neighbours.

spotlights.name: Joseph Hooker, the botanist who was taken hostage
spotlights.spot_it: A Victorian scientist with side-whiskers; or the hand-coloured plates of his book of Sikkim rhododendrons.
spotlights.story_md: In 1848 the young British botanist Joseph Dalton Hooker walked into Sikkim to collect plants. With Archibald Campbell, the British superintendent of Darjeeling, he was seized by the Sikkim court in 1849. Britain answered with a punitive expedition and annexed the Terai lowlands and more of the Darjeeling hills, and by the Treaty of Tumlong in 1861 Sikkim became a British protectorate in all but name. Hooker's seeds, sent to Kew, and his illustrated *Rhododendrons of Sikkim-Himalaya* set off a craze for the plants in British gardens. He later ran Kew for twenty years.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A plant-hunting trip ended with Sikkim losing land and sovereignty, and Britain gaining a garden obsession.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every rhododendron in an English park has a Sikkim hostage story behind it.

sections.title: From kingdom to the 22nd state
sections.intro_md:
When the British left India in 1947, Sikkim was neither a princely state nor a colony. A 1950 treaty made it an Indian protectorate: India ran defence, foreign affairs and communications, and the Chogyal ran the rest. That arrangement came apart over the next 25 years. The Nepali-speaking majority wanted democracy; the last Chogyal, Palden Thondup Namgyal, wanted more independence, not less; and India, after the 1962 war with China, wanted no doubt about the border.

In 1973 crowds besieged the palace. In 1974 the Sikkim National Congress of Kazi Lhendup Dorjee won 31 of 32 seats. In April 1975 Indian troops disarmed the palace guard, the assembly abolished the monarchy and a referendum endorsed it. On 16 May 1975 Sikkim became India's 22nd state. Whether that was liberation or annexation is still argued, inside Sikkim and out.

spotlights.name: Palden Thondup Namgyal, the last Chogyal
spotlights.spot_it: A slight man in a brocade robe and a Tibetan hat, often photographed beside his American queen.
spotlights.story_md: The twelfth and last Chogyal came to the throne in 1965, already long involved in running the kingdom for his father. He wanted Sikkim to be treated like Bhutan, a small independent Himalayan kingdom with its own seat in the world. India, which ran Sikkim's defence and foreign affairs under a 1950 treaty, did not. In 1973 protests against his rule spread across Gangtok; India stepped in; within two years elections, a new constitution and a referendum had abolished his throne. He died of cancer in New York in 1982.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His fight to keep Sikkim separate, and his loss, is how Sikkim became Indian.
spotlights.memory_hook: He wanted to be Bhutan; he ended up a state.

spotlights.name: Hope Cooke, the American queen
spotlights.spot_it: A slim young American woman in a Sikkimese bakhu and Tibetan jewellery, posing in front of a palace.
spotlights.story_md: Hope Cooke was a student from San Francisco, not yet 20, when she met the widowed crown prince at the Windamere Hotel in Darjeeling in 1959. They married in Gangtok on 20 March 1963, a year late because astrologers judged 1962 inauspicious, and she became Gyalmo, queen, at his coronation in 1965. She wrote for the *Bulletin of Tibetology* and became an international face of the kingdom. In July 1973, as protests grew, she left for New York with her children. She later wrote a memoir, *Time Change*, and became a historian of New York City.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She made Sikkim famous in the West, and in India her fame made the monarchy look foreign.
spotlights.memory_hook: A San Francisco student who became a Himalayan queen, then a New York historian.

spotlights.name: Kazi Lhendup Dorjee, the first Chief Minister
spotlights.spot_it: An elderly man in a Sikkimese robe and spectacles, most often shown in black-and-white photos of the 1970s.
spotlights.story_md: Kazi Lhendup Dorjee was born in Pakyong in 1904 into a noble family, served as a lama and became head lama of Rumtek before turning to politics. His Sikkim National Congress won 31 of 32 seats in 1974, and as Prime Minister he steered the assembly to depose the Chogyal and join India. He then became Sikkim's first Chief Minister, 1975 to 1979. Later he lost power, lived in Kalimpong, and received the Padma Vibhushan in 2002. He died in 2007, aged 102. In Sikkim his legacy is still argued over.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He was the Sikkimese face of the merger with India.
spotlights.memory_hook: A former lama who ended a monarchy and lived to 102.

spotlights.name: The 1975 referendum
spotlights.spot_it: The palace complex in Gangtok, its royal chapel the Tsuklakhang, where the monarchy ended.
spotlights.story_md: On 9 April 1975 Indian troops disarmed the Chogyal's palace guard. The same day the Sikkim assembly declared the monarchy abolished and asked to join India. A referendum on 14 April recorded 59,637 votes for and 1,496 against: **97.55%**, on a turnout of about 63%. Parliament passed the amendment in April and Sikkim became India's 22nd state on **16 May 1975**, now Statehood Day. Critics then and since have questioned how polling in remote villages was organised in days, and in 1978 Prime Minister Morarji Desai called the annexation 'not a desirable step'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the hinge of modern Sikkim, celebrated as a choice and still questioned as a takeover.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five weeks from a disarmed palace to a new Indian state.

sections.title: Who lives here, and what they speak
sections.intro_md:
Sikkim is three histories in one small state. The Lepcha are the oldest people. The Bhutia gave it its kings and its Buddhism. The Nepali-speaking communities, Rai, Limbu, Tamang, Gurung, Sherpa, Newar, Bahun, Chhetri and others, arrived in large numbers from the 19th century and are now about two-thirds of the population.

The state handles this by naming them all. It has 12 official languages and protects older residents through Article 371F, special land rules and the old 'Sikkim Subject' register. One of the 32 assembly seats, the Sangha seat, is reserved for Buddhist monks and nuns, the only such seat in India. These protections are also a source of tension, especially over who counts as Sikkimese and who gets jobs, land and tax exemptions.

spotlights.name: The Bhutia (Sikkimese)
spotlights.when: Arrived from Kham, Tibet, from about the 14th century
spotlights.spot_it: Women in a long wrap-around bakhu dress with a silk blouse and a striped apron for married women; men in a belted bakhu.
spotlights.story_md: The Bhutia (not to be confused with the people of Bhutan) came south from Kham in Tibet from around the 14th century. Their aristocracy gave Sikkim its kings, its monasteries and its state religion of Vajrayana Buddhism, and their language, Sikkimese or Drenjongke, is written in Tibetan script. Today they are a minority, about 7% of speakers in 2011. In North Sikkim the Lachenpa and Lachungpa still run their villages through the dzumsa, a council led by an elected headman called the pipon.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The kingdom's ruling culture, now one community among many in a democratic state.
spotlights.memory_hook: The kings' people became a minority in their own kingdom.

spotlights.name: The Nepali-speaking majority

where.label: All of Sikkim, most densely in the south and east

spotlights.when: Mostly arrived in the 19th and early 20th centuries
spotlights.spot_it: Men in a daura-suruwal and a Dhaka-cloth topi cap; women in a cholo blouse with a red shawl; Dashain tika on the forehead.
spotlights.story_md: Nepali is the first language of 62.6% of Sikkim. Its speakers include many peoples, Rai, Limbu, Tamang, Gurung, Sherpa, Newar, Bahun and Chhetri, who settled the hills in large numbers from the 1800s, when British officials encouraged them to clear land and grow crops. By the early 20th century they were the majority. That shift is the hidden story behind 1975: a majority that wanted democracy over a Buddhist monarchy. Nepali is now the state's main working language, and Dashain and Tihar are its biggest festivals.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Demography, not only diplomacy, turned a Buddhist kingdom into an Indian state.
spotlights.memory_hook: The settlers the British invited became the voters who ended the kingdom.

spotlights.name: The Limbu and their book of the world
spotlights.spot_it: Dancers in a line beating large two-headed chyabrung drums slung at the hip, stepping in a slow circle.
spotlights.story_md: The Limbu, who call themselves Yakthung, are among the oldest peoples of Sikkim and eastern Nepal. Their faith rests on the Mundhum, an oral scripture recited by priests that covers creation, marriage and death. They have their own script, Sirijanga. The chyabrung drum dance is their signature, and tongba, warm millet beer sipped through a bamboo straw, is their drink of hospitality: offering it is a mark of respect, and a newly married couple share it at the wedding. Limbu is one of Sikkim's official languages.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They show that 'Nepali' in Sikkim covers peoples with scripts and scriptures of their own.
spotlights.memory_hook: A whole worldview kept in a recited book, and served with millet beer.

spotlights.name: Lepcha script
spotlights.spot_it: Rounded letters with small hooks and dots written on a line, unlike the angular Tibetan script around it.
spotlights.story_md: The Lepcha script, Róng, is one of the oldest scripts of the eastern Himalaya, developed in the 17th to 18th centuries and influenced by Tibetan writing. It was used for Buddhist texts and folk literature. Missionaries printed it in the 19th century and the Sikkim government teaches it in schools today. It is one of the 12 official languages in a state of about six lakh people, which may make Sikkim the most multilingual state per head in India: Nepali, Sikkimese, Lepcha, Limbu, Newar, Gurung, Magar, Rai, Sherpa, Tamang, Sunwar and Bhujel.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A small state that legally keeps 12 languages is making a choice about who belongs.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twelve official languages for fewer people than a Delhi suburb.

sections.title: Monasteries, temples and the wind
sections.intro_md:
The first thing visitors notice is the Buddhism: prayer flags on every bridge, monasteries on every ridge, giant golden statues above the clouds. The census says something else. In 2011 **57.8%** of Sikkim was Hindu, **27.4%** Buddhist and **9.9%** Christian, the fastest-growing group, up from 6.7% in 2001. The state counted 336 Hindu temples, 168 churches and about a hundred monasteries.

What makes Sikkim distinctive is how much the faiths overlap. Hindu families hang prayer flags; Buddhists visit the Char Dham temples at Namchi; Lepcha shamans and lamas perform at the same funeral. Sikkimese Buddhism itself is mostly Nyingma, the oldest Tibetan school, centred on Guru Rinpoche, with the Karma Kagyu seat at Rumtek a powerful later arrival.

spotlights.name: Rumtek Monastery
spotlights.spot_it: A big, bright monastery with a red, yellow and green facade, gold roof ornaments and armed police at the gate.
spotlights.story_md: When the 16th Karmapa, head of the Karma Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism, fled Tibet in 1959, the Chogyal offered him land. He rebuilt an older monastery at Rumtek and inaugurated it at Losar in 1966 as his seat in exile. A golden stupa holds his relics. After his death in 1981 two rival candidates were recognised as the 17th Karmapa, and their supporters fought in courts and in the courtyard. Neither candidate lives at Rumtek, and security forces have patrolled it since 2003.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most important Tibetan Buddhist seat in India outside Dharamshala, and one of its most contested.
spotlights.memory_hook: A monastery waiting for a Karmapa who never comes.

spotlights.name: Pemayangtse Monastery
spotlights.spot_it: A three-storey whitewashed monastery with a red-trimmed roof on a ridge at 2,085 m, facing Kangchenjunga.
spotlights.story_md: Pemayangtse, 'perfect sublime lotus', was founded in 1647 by Lhatsun Chempo, one of the three lamas who crowned the first king, and enlarged in 1705. It is a Nyingma monastery, and only its monks may hold the title of ta-tshang, 'pure monks', traditionally drawn from Bhutia families. Its head lama anointed the Chogyals. Its roof is chained to the floor against monsoon winds, a fix after earthquakes in 1913 and 1960. Each February its masked cham dance closes the Tibetan year with fireworks.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The royal monastery: the place that made kings legitimate.
spotlights.memory_hook: The monastery whose monks crowned kings, with its roof chained down.

spotlights.name: Tashiding and the Bumchu vase
spotlights.when: Founded 1641; Bumchu each February or March
spotlights.spot_it: A hilltop monastery between two rivers, crowded with chortens and pilgrims queuing for a spoonful of holy water.
spotlights.story_md: Tashiding, founded in 1641, is called the heart of Sikkim. Once a year, on the 14th and 15th of the first Tibetan month, lamas open a sealed vase of water said to have been hidden by Guru Padmasambhava and read the coming year from it. A full or half-full vase means prosperity; a low level means famine; dusty water means strife. Then the water is shared with pilgrims, and the vase is topped up from the river and sealed for another year. Its Thongwa Rangdrol chorten is believed to free anyone who simply sees it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a state-wide forecast, read from a pot, that thousands still travel to hear.
spotlights.memory_hook: A whole state's weather report, read from a single vase.

spotlights.name: Enchey Monastery
spotlights.spot_it: A compact Chinese-pagoda-style monastery in a grove of tall pines on a ridge above Gangtok, ringed by prayer flags.
spotlights.story_md: Enchey was built in 1909, under the Chogyal Thutob Namgyal, on a site blessed by a tantric master said to have flown here. It belongs to the Nyingma school. Its fame is its winter cham, a masked dance held around the end of the Tibetan year, when monks in masks of protector deities and skeletons dance in the courtyard and the town crowds the walls to watch. Old film from the mid-20th century shows the same dances almost unchanged.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the monastery of Gangtok itself and the easiest place to see a cham.
spotlights.memory_hook: Gangtok's guardian sits in a pine grove and dances in skull masks once a year.

spotlights.name: Do Drul Chorten
spotlights.spot_it: A large white stupa with a gold spire, surrounded by a ring of red prayer wheels that pilgrims spin as they walk clockwise.
spotlights.story_md: Do Drul Chorten in Gangtok was built in 1945 by Trulshik Rinpoche, a lama of the Nyingma school, to subdue spirits said to trouble the area. It holds relics, texts and mantras inside, and is ringed by 108 prayer wheels. Each spin of a wheel is believed to send out the prayers printed and rolled inside it. People walk round it clockwise, always, keeping the stupa on their right, often while counting beads. It is the most visited stupa in the state.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where you see everyday Buddhist practice in Sikkim: walking, spinning, counting.
spotlights.memory_hook: 108 wheels, one direction, never anticlockwise.

spotlights.name: Buddha Park, Ravangla
spotlights.spot_it: A 40 m golden-copper seated Buddha on a high lawn above the clouds, with the snow range behind it on clear days.
spotlights.story_md: The Buddha at Ravangla is about 40 m tall and made from roughly 60 tonnes of copper beaten into shape. It was built to mark the 2,550th birth anniversary of the Buddha and consecrated by the Dalai Lama on 25 March 2013. It is part of a deliberate strategy: Sikkim has spent heavily on giant religious statues and parks to spread tourists beyond Gangtok, and South Sikkim has three such landmarks within an hour of each other, the Ravangla Buddha, the Guru Rinpoche statue at Namchi, and the Char Dham Hindu complex.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Faith as infrastructure: big statues are how South Sikkim built a tourism economy.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sixty tonnes of copper hammered into calm.

spotlights.name: Guru Rinpoche statue, Samdruptse, Namchi
spotlights.spot_it: A giant seated figure in gold, copper and red robes, holding a vajra and a skull-cup, on a forested hilltop above Namchi.
spotlights.story_md: Guru Rinpoche, Padmasambhava, is the 8th-century tantric master who in Sikkimese belief blessed the land, hid sacred texts in its lakes and caves, and foretold the coming of its kings. His statue on Samdruptse hill above Namchi, completed in 2004, is about 45 m tall, among the tallest of him anywhere. He is everywhere in Sikkim: in the legend of Gurudongmar, the Bumchu vase at Tashiding, the wrathful image at Pemayangtse. If one figure explains Sikkimese Buddhism, it is him.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The saint who, in local belief, wrote Sikkim's future before it had a king.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Guru who left Sikkim his footprints, his water and his prophecies.

spotlights.name: Prayer flags and white manidar
spotlights.spot_it: Strings of blue, white, red, green and yellow cloth squares across bridges and passes; tall white flags on poles in rows.
spotlights.story_md: The coloured flags are lungta, wind horses, printed with prayers that the wind is believed to carry out across the land. The five colours stand for space, air, fire, water and earth, always in that order. They are put up on auspicious days and left to fade, since fading is part of the point. The tall white flags in rows, often on hillsides above a road, are for the dead. Families raise them, traditionally 108 of them, after a death, so the prayers carry the person forward.
spotlights.why_it_matters: This is the most visible sign of Buddhism in Sikkim, even in Hindu-majority towns.
spotlights.memory_hook: Prayers printed on cloth and handed to the wind.

sections.title: Masks, scrolls and carpets
sections.intro_md:
Most of Sikkim's classical art is religious and comes from the monasteries: the cham masked dance, thangka scroll paintings, murals, butter sculptures and ritual music on long horns and drums. Folk art is just as varied. The Lepcha have their own songs and dance-dramas built around Kangchenjunga; the Limbu dance to the big chyabrung drum; Nepali communities have the maruni and tamang selo.

The government's Directorate of Handicrafts and Handloom, set up in Gangtok in 1957, trains young people in thangka painting, woodcarving, carpet weaving and Lepcha weaving, which keeps crafts alive that might otherwise have stayed inside a few families.

spotlights.name: Cham, the masked dance

where.label: Monastery courtyards: Rumtek, Enchey, Pemayangtse, Tsuklakhang

spotlights.when: Mostly around the Tibetan new year
spotlights.spot_it: Monks in huge painted masks and swirling brocade robes turn slowly to cymbals, long horns and drums in a monastery courtyard.
spotlights.story_md: Cham is a ritual dance-drama performed by monks, and in Sikkim also by lay dancers. The dancers become deities: wrathful protectors, skeleton lords of the cremation ground, the eight forms of Guru Rinpoche. The movements are slow, heavy, spinning, and every step is a meditation. Many dances end with the destruction of an effigy that stands for evil or bad luck, so the community enters the new year clean. In the Pang Lhabsol cham, the mountain god Kangchenjunga appears as a dancer in a red mask crowned with five skulls.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is how Sikkimese Buddhism teaches by spectacle: theology as theatre.
spotlights.memory_hook: Monks in skull masks sweeping the old year out of the courtyard.

spotlights.name: Thangka painting

where.label: Directorate of Handicrafts and Handloom, Gangtok

spotlights.spot_it: A painted cloth scroll framed in silk brocade, showing a deity in the centre surrounded by tiny figures, in mineral blues, reds and gold.
spotlights.story_md: A thangka is a Buddhist painting on cotton, framed in silk, that can be rolled up and carried. Every proportion follows a grid set by canonical texts, so a painter spends years learning to draw a Buddha before being allowed to invent anything. Pigments were traditionally ground from minerals and gold. Thangkas are teaching tools, meditation aids and offerings. In Gangtok the government's Directorate of Handicrafts and Handloom, set up in 1957, still trains young painters alongside carpet weavers and woodcarvers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the visual language of every monastery in the state.
spotlights.memory_hook: A painting you can roll up, ruled by a grid older than the kingdom.

spotlights.name: Carpets and carved choktse tables
spotlights.spot_it: Thick hand-knotted woollen carpets with dragons, snow lions and lotus borders on deep blue, red or ochre grounds.
spotlights.story_md: Carpets in Sikkim follow the Tibetan tradition: hand-knotted wool, woven on upright looms, in patterns of dragons, snow lions, cranes and endless knots. They were made to cover the low benches and floors of houses and monasteries in a cold climate. Weaving centres in Gangtok and the refugee settlements of the 1960s brought more Tibetan weavers into the state. In Lachen and Lachung, families still weave their own on home looms. The same workshops make the choktse, a low folding table carved with dragons and lotuses and painted bright, used for scriptures, tea and meals on the floor.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A craft that keeps old Tibetan design alive inside India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Dragons you sit on.

sections.title: Momos, fermented greens and stone-hard cheese
sections.intro_md:
Sikkimese food is mountain food: built for cold, for altitude and for long winters when roads close. It is much closer to Tibet and Nepal than to Bengal next door. Rice is the base, but noodles, dumplings and fermented foods are everywhere: greens are soured and dried into gundruk, radish into sinki, milk into chhurpi, millet into tongba beer.

Meat is common, especially pork and beef among Bhutia and Nepali families. Chilli is serious. A Padmasambhava text quoted by the state lists 155 fruits and 360 edible plants, a sign of how much the forest feeds the kitchen.

spotlights.name: Momo
spotlights.spot_it: Pleated steamed dumplings, half-moon or round, served in a steel steamer with a fiery red tomato-chilli sauce and clear soup.
spotlights.story_md: Momos came over the Himalaya with Tibetan and Newar traders and became the default snack of the eastern Himalaya, then of all urban India. In Sikkim they come with pork, beef, chicken, cheese or vegetable fillings, steamed, fried or dropped into soup. The sauce matters as much as the dumpling: tomato, garlic and the local Dalle chilli. Gangtok's MG Marg and lanes behind it are thick with momo shops. The dish is so central that tourists often learn to say 'momo' before 'thank you'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Momos are how much of India first tastes the Himalaya.
spotlights.memory_hook: A pleat, a steam, a burn.

spotlights.name: Thukpa
spotlights.spot_it: A deep bowl of noodle soup with vegetables or meat in a clear broth, eaten with chopsticks and a spoon.
spotlights.story_md: Thukpa is the Tibetan word for noodle soup, and in Sikkim it is a meal, not a starter. There are several kinds: thukpa with long noodles, thenthuk with hand-pulled flat pieces torn into the pot, gyathuk, a richer 'Chinese' version. At 2,000 m and above, a hot bowl in the evening is close to a necessity. Wikipedia's list of Sikkim noodles also includes chow mein and wonton, showing how the food of the state faces north and east as much as south.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A daily dish that shows Sikkim's food is closer to Tibet than to Bengal.
spotlights.memory_hook: Soup with noodles torn by hand into the pot.

spotlights.name: Gundruk and sinki
spotlights.spot_it: Dark, dry, crinkled strips of fermented greens, cooked into a sour soup or pickle.
spotlights.story_md: Gundruk is made from the leaves of mustard, radish or cauliflower. They are wilted, shredded, packed tight in an earthen pot or a pit for a week or two to ferment, then sun-dried. Sinki does the same with radish roots. The result keeps for months, which matters in a place where fresh greens vanish in winter and roads close. Cooked as a sour soup with rice, it is the taste of home for Nepali-speaking families across the Himalaya. It is a reminder that fermentation, not refrigeration, built mountain cuisines.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A preservation technology disguised as a soup.
spotlights.memory_hook: Leaves buried, soured, dried and saved for winter.

spotlights.name: Sel roti
spotlights.spot_it: A thin golden ring of fried rice-flour batter, crisp outside and soft inside, stacked high on a plate.
spotlights.story_md: Sel roti is made from ground soaked rice, sugar, ghee and sometimes banana, poured by hand in a smooth circle into hot oil. Getting a perfect ring is a skill learned by watching. It is the festival bread of Nepali families: stacks are made for Tihar and Dashain, given to relatives and guests and eaten with tea, curd or meat. Because it keeps well for days, it is also travel food.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The food that marks a festival in most Sikkimese households.
spotlights.memory_hook: A ring poured by hand into oil, once a year, by the hundred.

spotlights.name: Chhurpi, the hardest cheese
spotlights.spot_it: Small, pale, rock-hard cubes strung on a cord, or soft crumbly white cheese mixed into chutney.
spotlights.story_md: Chhurpi comes in two kinds. Soft chhurpi is made from boiled buttermilk, drained in cloth and eaten in curries, soups and momos. Hard chhurpi is the same cheese pressed, dried, cut into cubes and smoked over a fire until it is like stone. You do not bite it: you hold a cube in your mouth until it softens, and one piece can last from half an hour to five hours. It is said to be one of the hardest cheeses in the world. Nepal now exports it as dog chews, a business worth about Rs 4 billion in 2025.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A herder's way to carry milk for months, now a pet-shop export.
spotlights.memory_hook: A cheese you suck for an hour before it lets you chew.

spotlights.name: Tongba, millet beer

where.label: Limbu and Rai homes, West Sikkim

spotlights.spot_it: A wooden or bamboo mug packed with fermented millet, topped up with hot water and sipped through a bamboo straw.
spotlights.story_md: Tongba is the name of the vessel as much as the drink. Finger millet is cooked, mixed with a starter culture called marcha and left to ferment. To serve, the fermented grain is packed into the tongba, hot water poured over and left a few minutes, then sipped through a bamboo straw whose end filters out the grain. When it runs dry the host adds more hot water. It is mild, about 2 to 5% alcohol. Among the Limbu it is the drink of guests and weddings.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A beer you refill with a kettle, and the centre of Limbu hospitality.
spotlights.memory_hook: Beer made by pouring hot water on grain, again and again.

spotlights.name: Dalle khursani
spotlights.spot_it: A small round red cherry-shaped chilli, glossy and fat, usually pickled in oil or ground into a fierce paste.
spotlights.story_md: Dalle means round in Nepali, and the chilli looks like a cherry. It is among the hottest chillies grown in India, and a little goes a long way in a pickle or a momo sauce. It holds a Geographical Indication: reported in 2020 and certified in 2021, later extended to the neighbouring Darjeeling and Kalimpong hills. Like large cardamom, it suits small hillside farms, and it is one of the products Sikkim hopes to sell under its organic label.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A small farm crop with a big brand, and a test of whether organic can earn a premium.
spotlights.memory_hook: A cherry that bites back.

sections.title: A year of festivals
sections.intro_md:
Sikkim keeps three calendars at once: the Tibetan lunar year of the monasteries, the Hindu calendar of the Nepali majority, and the farming year. That makes for a crowded holiday list. Losar shuts offices for about a week around February; Saga Dawa is the holiest Buddhist day; Pang Lhabsol, unique to Sikkim, honours Kangchenjunga; Dashain and Tihar are the biggest Hindu festivals; Losoong closes the harvest year in December. Christmas and Eid are public holidays too.

Many festivals include masked dances in monastery courtyards, archery contests and a lot of chhaang and tongba.

spotlights.name: Losar, the Tibetan new year
spotlights.spot_it: Monasteries hung with new flags, families in their best bakhu, plates of fried khapse pastries and butter tea.
spotlights.story_md: Losar opens the Tibetan lunar year, usually in February or early March. In Sikkim it closes most offices and schools for about a week. The days before are for cleaning and for rites that drive out the old year's misfortune, including masked dances and the burning of effigies at Rumtek. Then come new clothes, visits, khapse pastries, chhaang beer and archery contests. Sherpa and Tamang communities keep their own new years, Losar and Sonam Lhosar, at slightly different dates.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the Buddhist calendar's reset button, and the state's biggest winter holiday.
spotlights.memory_hook: A whole week to throw out the old year.

spotlights.name: Losoong (Namsoong)
spotlights.spot_it: Monks in masks and archers in the same week: the Sikkimese harvest new year.
spotlights.story_md: Losoong is the new year of the Sikkimese Bhutia, falling at the end of the tenth Tibetan month, usually December, when the harvest is in. The Lepcha celebrate the same season as Namsoong. Monasteries hold cham dances to drive away evil before the new cycle, and villages hold archery contests, feasts and drinking of chhaang. Doordarshan's Gangtok station has filmed it for its archive. For farmers it is the real new year; Losar, two months later, belongs more to the monasteries.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how Buddhist ritual in Sikkim is tied to the farming year.
spotlights.memory_hook: When the rice is in, the year turns.

spotlights.name: Saga Dawa
spotlights.when: Full moon of the fourth Tibetan month, May or June
spotlights.spot_it: A long procession of monks carrying wrapped holy books on their backs through Gangtok, with horns and cymbals ahead.
spotlights.story_md: Saga Dawa marks three events in the Buddha's life at once: his birth, his enlightenment and his death and passing into nirvana. In Sikkim it is the holiest day of the year. Monks carry the scriptures out of the monasteries and through the streets of Gangtok in a procession; people give alms, release animals, avoid meat and light butter lamps. Merit gained this month is believed to be multiplied many times, so even people who rarely visit a monastery make an effort now.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The holiest Buddhist day, celebrated in public, in a Hindu-majority state.
spotlights.memory_hook: Birth, awakening and death on one full moon.

spotlights.name: Pang Lhabsol
spotlights.when: 15th day of the seventh Tibetan month, August or September
spotlights.spot_it: Lay dancers in armour, helmets and swords leap in a palace courtyard, around a figure in a red mask with five skulls.
spotlights.story_md: Pang Lhabsol is unique to Sikkim. It honours Kangchenjunga as the guardian deity of the land and remembers an oath of brotherhood said to have been sworn in the 13th century between the Bhutia chief Khye Bumsa and the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek, with the mountain as witness. Its centrepiece is a warrior dance, pangtoed, performed not by monks but by young laymen, and a masked dance in which the mountain god himself appears. It is a festival of unity between peoples as much as of faith.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the one festival that ties the Lepcha, the Bhutia and the mountain into a single story.
spotlights.memory_hook: A festival where the guest of honour is a mountain.

sections.title: How people live
sections.intro_md:
Survey data paints Sikkim as unusual for India. It is mostly rural, about three-quarters village, but well-off: first among states on income per head. It was among the first states declared free of open defecation, literacy is above 80%, and it has the lowest fertility rate of any state. Women run a large share of the shops and market stalls in Gangtok.

It is also a state of rules. Gangtok fines spitting and littering, plastic is restricted, and the whole state farms organically by law. Those rules are a source of pride, and of complaints from farmers and traders. Two worries run underneath: a shrinking, ageing indigenous population, and fragile slopes that are being built on fast.

spotlights.name: India's first fully organic state
spotlights.spot_it: Narrow green terraces cut into steep slopes, with a hand-lettered sign about organic farming at the village edge.
spotlights.story_md: Sikkim began phasing out chemical fertilisers and pesticides in 2003, set up an Organic Mission in 2010, and in January 2016 Prime Minister Modi declared it India's first fully organic state, with about 75,000 hectares certified. Selling or using chemical pesticides was banned. In 2018 the policy won the Future Policy Gold Award, given by the World Future Council with the UN's FAO, ahead of 51 other nominees. Since then the hard part has been yields and prices: farmers say organic has not always paid, and the state still buys much of its food from the plains.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the world's most famous test of whether a whole state can farm without chemicals.
spotlights.memory_hook: A state that banned the pesticide shelf.

spotlights.name: MG Marg, Gangtok
spotlights.spot_it: A clean paved promenade with benches, flower boxes and no cars, lined with shops, cafes and momo stalls.
spotlights.story_md: Mahatma Gandhi Marg is Gangtok's main street and its showroom. Cars are banned, and so are littering, spitting and smoking, rules that are enforced and that most people follow. In the evening half the town walks it. It is the visible face of a state that likes to be first in cleanliness lists: Sikkim banned plastic bags early, banned bottled water at government events in 2016, and was among the first states to be declared free of open defecation. It is also where tourists notice that Gangtok has rules Delhi does not.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the everyday proof of Sikkim's civic culture.
spotlights.memory_hook: A main street where you can be fined for spitting, and people actually aren't.

spotlights.name: Mero Rukh Mero Santati: trees for every baby
spotlights.spot_it: Parents planting a row of saplings with a small sign carrying their child's name.
spotlights.story_md: In 2023 the Sikkim government launched Mero Rukh Mero Santati, 'my tree, my child'. Families who register a newborn by sending a greeting to a WhatsApp number are given saplings to plant in the child's name: 100 per child in the launch coverage, 108 on the forest department's own site. It sits alongside other measures from the same years aimed at a falling birth rate, including extra pay increments for government employees with a second or third child and a Rs 3 lakh grant for mothers who conceive through IVF.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It joins two of Sikkim's preoccupations: forests and a shrinking population.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hundred trees for every baby.

spotlights.name: The lowest birth rate in India
spotlights.spot_it: A number, not a picture: 1.1 children per woman.
spotlights.story_md: The National Family Health Survey of 2019 to 2020 found Sikkim's total fertility rate at **1.1** children per woman, the lowest of any Indian state and far below the replacement level of about 2.1. In 1998 to 1999 it had been 2.75. That is a European or East Asian pattern in a Himalayan state. Fear that indigenous communities would shrink led the government in 2023 to offer extra increments to employees with two or three children, IVF grants, and childcare attendants at home for new mothers in government jobs.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Sikkim is a preview of the demographic future many Indian states are heading towards.
spotlights.memory_hook: One child per woman: Seoul numbers in the Himalaya.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
Sikkim's famous names are few but distinctive: a striker who refused the Olympic torch, an actor who became Bollywood's best villain and a brewer, and a poet-politician who ran the state for nearly a quarter of a century. Earlier chapters met the others: the last Chogyal and his American queen, and Kazi Lhendup Dorjee, who took Sikkim into India.

The current Chief Minister is Prem Singh Tamang, known as P. S. Golay, whose Sikkim Krantikari Morcha won 31 of 32 seats in June 2024.

spotlights.name: Bhaichung Bhutia
spotlights.spot_it: A compact striker in India's blue shirt, celebrating with both arms out.
spotlights.story_md: Born in 1976 in Tinkitam, Bhaichung Bhutia became the face of Indian football for fifteen years. In 1999 he signed for Bury in England, the first Indian footballer signed by a European club in the modern era, and he played 83 times for India with 27 goals by the stats tables. He earned the nickname 'the Sikkimese Sniper' and the Padma Shri in 2008. That year he refused to carry the Olympic torch in India in support of Tibet. A stadium in Namchi bears his name, and he has since tried politics, founding the Hamro Sikkim Party in 2018.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He made a tiny state famous in India's biggest crowd sport.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Sikkimese Sniper who said no to the Olympic torch.

spotlights.name: Danny Denzongpa
spotlights.spot_it: A Bollywood actor with a lean face and a menacing calm, best known for villain roles like Kancha Cheena in Agneepath.
spotlights.story_md: Tshering Phintso Denzongpa was born in Yuksom in 1948, the village where Sikkim's first king was crowned. At the Film and Television Institute in Pune his classmate Jaya Bhaduri suggested he use 'Danny', since few could pronounce his name. He became one of Hindi cinema's great villains, Kancha Cheena in *Agneepath* (1990) above all, and won the Padma Shri in 2003. In 1987 he set up Yuksom Breweries in Sikkim, which grew into the biggest brewery in north-east India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: For decades, he was the most famous Sikkimese face on Indian screens.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bollywood's best villain runs a brewery back home.

spotlights.name: Pawan Kumar Chamling
spotlights.spot_it: A smiling politician in a Nepali topi and white kurta, usually photographed at a rally or a book launch.
spotlights.story_md: Pawan Kumar Chamling founded the Sikkim Democratic Front in 1993 and was Chief Minister from 12 December 1994 to May 2019, about 24 and a half years, making him the longest-serving chief minister in India's history. Under him Sikkim went organic, built hydropower dams and pharma factories, and climbed to the top of per-capita income tables. He is also a Nepali poet who won the Bhanu Puraskar in 2010. In 2019 his party lost; in June 2024 he lost both seats he contested, his first personal defeat.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He shaped modern Sikkim more than anyone since 1975.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty-four years in charge, then two seats lost in one day.

sections.title: Passes, roads and treks
sections.intro_md:
Most visitors base themselves in Gangtok and make three trips: east to Tsomgo Lake and Nathu La, north to Lachung, Yumthang and Gurudongmar, and west to Pelling, Yuksom and the monasteries. Much of the north and east is a restricted border zone, so Indians need permits for many places and foreigners need a Protected Area Permit; some areas are closed to foreigners entirely.

The best seasons are March to May, when rhododendrons flower, and October to December, when the mountains are clearest. In the monsoon, June to September, landslides close roads for days at a time.

pins.label: Yuksom, start of the Goecha La trek

spotlights.name: Nathu La
spotlights.spot_it: A wind-blasted pass at about 4,300 m with a border fence, Indian and Chinese soldiers a few metres apart, and snow most of the year.
spotlights.story_md: Nathu La was a branch of the old trade route between Lhasa and the plains, carrying wool, mules and salt one way and cloth and sugar the other. Trade stopped after the 1962 war. In September 1967 Indian and Chinese troops fought here for several days over a wire fence, the last major clash until 2020. Border trade reopened in 2006 and was suspended in 2020. On 1 August 2026 it reopened again after six years, with 38 licensed traders and about 35 kinds of goods. Visitors need a permit and go only on set days.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where geopolitics in Sikkim is literally a few metres wide.
spotlights.memory_hook: A pass where soldiers can almost shake hands, and sometimes trade.

spotlights.name: Baba Harbhajan Singh's shrine

where.label: Between Sherathang and Kupup, near Nathu La

spotlights.spot_it: A small yellow-and-red shrine on a high road, filled with boots, uniforms and bottles of water left by visitors.
spotlights.story_md: Harbhajan Singh was a 22-year-old sepoy of the Punjab Regiment who died near Nathu La in October 1968, said to have fallen into a stream while escorting mules. Soldiers came to believe he still guards the border, warning them in dreams. His shrine, Baba Mandir, gets bottles of water left overnight to be blessed. Every year on 11 September his belongings are sent by train to his village in Punjab, with an empty seat booked for him and soldiers as escorts. A 2018 short film, *Plus Minus*, was loosely based on him.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how soldiers on a lonely frontier build their own faith.
spotlights.memory_hook: The soldier who, in the army's telling, never went off duty.

spotlights.name: Zuluk and the Old Silk Route
spotlights.when: Road built for the border; tourists since the 2010s
spotlights.spot_it: A mountain road folding back on itself in dozens of tight hairpin loops, seen from above like a thrown ribbon.
spotlights.story_md: Zuluk is a tiny village at about 2,900 m on the old mule route from Kalimpong to Lhasa through the Jelep La pass. Today it is famous for the road above it, which zigzags up the slope in roughly 30 hairpin bends to Thambi viewpoint, one of the most photographed roads in India. The route, now called the Old Silk Route by tourism boards, passes army camps and needs a permit. Homestays in Zuluk are run by village families who used to live off the mule trade.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a frontier road turned into a tourist attraction.
spotlights.memory_hook: A road that looks like a dropped piece of string.

spotlights.name: Dzongri and Goecha La trek

where.label: From Yuksom into Khangchendzonga National Park

spotlights.when: Best April to May and October to November
spotlights.spot_it: A high moraine pass at the foot of Kangchenjunga's south face, prayer flags on a cairn, reached before dawn by head-torch.
spotlights.story_md: The trek from Yuksom to Goecha La is the classic way to stand face to face with Kangchenjunga without climbing it. It takes about a week, through rhododendron forest to the Dzongri meadows and on past the lake at Samiti to a pass at about 4,600 to 4,900 m. Trekkers set off around 3 am to reach the viewpoint for sunrise on the south-east face. It runs through the national park, so there are permits, fees and limits, and in some seasons the route is closed after floods or landslides.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most famous trek in eastern India.
spotlights.memory_hook: A week's walk to say good morning to the third highest mountain.

spotlights.name: Lachung and the dzumsa
spotlights.spot_it: Wooden houses with stone foundations in a deep valley under huge cliffs and waterfalls, apple trees in the gardens.
spotlights.story_md: Lachung, 125 km north of Gangtok, is the base for Yumthang Valley and Zero Point. It is also one of the few places in India with its own traditional government recognised by the state: the dzumsa. Every household sends a member; the council elects a headman, the pipon, settles disputes, fixes grazing dates and fines people who break the rules. The neighbouring village of Lachen runs the same system, and since 1995 state law has treated each dzumsa as the village panchayat. In 2025 the pipon elections turned into scuffles, a sign that party politics is reaching it too.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a working example of village self-rule older than Indian democracy.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Himalayan village with its own parliament and its own fines.

sections.title: How a farming state got rich
sections.intro_md:
For most of its history Sikkim lived on rice, maize, cardamom, oranges and trade over the passes. Today it ranks first among Indian states in income per head, but the reasons are recent: tax breaks for industry in the north-east drew more than 50 pharma companies; hydropower dams on the Teesta sell electricity to the grid; and tourism, much of it from West Bengal, has grown fast.

The income is real but narrow. Pharma plants are owned outside the state, dams carry risks the 2023 flood made plain, and tourism depends on one highway, NH10, which landslides cut several times a year. The state's own farming brands, organic produce, large cardamom, Temi tea, Dalle chilli, are small earners with big names.

spotlights.name: Large cardamom

where.label: Shaded hill slopes, mostly South and West Sikkim

spotlights.spot_it: Tall leafy clumps under alder trees, with dark red-brown pods clustered at ground level; then smoky black dried pods.
spotlights.story_md: Sikkim grows more large cardamom than any other Indian state. Unlike green cardamom, it grows in clumps on the forest floor under shade trees, usually Himalayan alder, and the pods are dried over wood fires in kilns called bhatti, which gives them their smoky, camphor taste. It is a key note in North Indian garam masala and biryanis. Nepal is the world's biggest producer, India second. Sikkim large cardamom was the state's first GI tag, in 2015. Viral diseases and old plantations have cut yields since the 1990s.
spotlights.why_it_matters: For generations it was the hill farmer's cash crop, grown without clearing forest.
spotlights.memory_hook: A spice that grows under trees and tastes of smoke.

spotlights.name: Temi Tea Garden
spotlights.spot_it: Neat rows of tea bushes curving round a single hillside, with Kangchenjunga visible behind on clear days.
spotlights.story_md: Temi is the only tea estate in Sikkim. It was set up in 1969 under the last Chogyal on about 177 hectares of slope below the Tendong hill, and it is run by the state. It converted to organic methods from 2005, using manure, neem cake and vermicompost. It produces about 100 tonnes of tea a year, small next to neighbouring Darjeeling, but its first-flush teas sell at premium prices in auctions. Cherry trees line the approach road and the estate is now a tourist stop too.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One estate carries the state's reputation in the tea world.
spotlights.memory_hook: One hill, one garden, one state's entire tea.

spotlights.name: Teesta dams

where.label: Teesta valley, North and East Sikkim

spotlights.spot_it: A concrete barrage across a narrow gorge with gates open, white water foaming below.
spotlights.story_md: Sikkim's slopes make it ideal for run-of-river hydropower: water is taken from the Teesta through tunnels and dropped onto turbines. NHPC's Teesta V (510 MW) has run since 2008, and Teesta III (1,200 MW), at Chungthang, opened in 2017 after costs rose from about Rs 5,700 crore to over Rs 14,000 crore. Power sales are a big part of the state's income. In October 2023 a glacial flood destroyed Teesta III; rebuilding at about twice the original dam height has been approved. Lepcha groups have fought dams in Dzongu since the early 2000s.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Hydropower pays Sikkim's bills and drives its fiercest arguments.
spotlights.memory_hook: Electricity from a river that sometimes takes the dam back.

spotlights.name: The pharma hub
spotlights.spot_it: Factory gates with familiar pharma company names along the Teesta near Rangpo.
spotlights.story_md: Tax breaks for the north-east, full exemption from income tax and excise plus capital subsidies from 2007, drew India's drug companies to a state with no history of industry. More than 50 pharmaceutical firms now operate in Sikkim, including Sun Pharma, Cipla, Zydus, Torrent, Mankind and Alkem, mostly in East Sikkim. An industry estimate once put the cluster at 10 to 13% of Indian pharma revenue. The plants are a main reason Sikkim tops per-capita income tables, though much of that income does not stay in local hands.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains how a small farming state ranks first in India on income per head.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pills from a valley that once only shipped cardamom.

sections.title: What is happening now
sections.intro_md:
Sikkim marked 50 years of statehood on 16 May 2025. The two years since have been busy and often harsh. The 2023 flood still shapes politics: the rebuilt Teesta III dam was approved at about twice the old height, and Lepcha groups are fighting a new dam, Teesta IV. In June 2025 a landslide hit an army camp at Chaten in North Sikkim, killing three and leaving six missing, and more than 1,500 tourists had to be evacuated from Lachen and Lachung. On 20 July 2026 an explosion in a tunnel at NHPC's Teesta Stage VI project in Namchi district killed between 20 and 25 workers.

There is good news too. Nathu La reopened for trade with China on 1 August 2026 after six years. The Sevoke-Rangpo railway, Sikkim's first, is expected around 2027. President Droupadi Murmu visited from 26 to 28 May 2026, including Nathu La.

spotlights.name: The South Lhonak flood, October 2023

where.label: South Lhonak Lake to Chungthang and beyond

spotlights.spot_it: Brown floodwater filling a valley floor where a dam and a town used to be, with twisted steel and mud-covered houses.
spotlights.story_md: South Lhonak was a glacial lake that had grown from 0.15 square km in 1975 to about 1.7 by 2023. Shortly after midnight on 4 October 2023, a mass of frozen moraine collapsed into it, and more than 50 million cubic metres of water burst out. The wave tore down the Teesta, destroyed the 1,200 MW Teesta III dam at Chungthang, took out 31 bridges and long sections of NH10, and flooded towns into West Bengal. A 2025 study counted 55 dead and 74 missing. Scientists had flagged this exact risk in 2021.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest warning yet of how warming turns Himalayan lakes into hazards.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lake that grew for 50 years and emptied in a night.

sections.title: Myths and what is true
sections.intro_md: Sikkim attracts myths because it is small, remote and was, until 1975, a kingdom most Indians knew only from stamps. Some popular beliefs are wrong, some half right, and a few are matters of faith that cannot be tested, which is not the same as false. The table below checks the most common ones against the census, the historical record and the reporting of the time. Where historians still disagree, as over how the 1975 referendum was run, the verdict says so rather than picking a side.

data.claim: Sikkim was always part of India
data.why: It was a kingdom from 1642, a British protectorate from 1861 and an Indian protectorate from 1950; it became a state in 1975.
Hindus are 57.8% and Buddhists 27.4% (2011), though Buddhism shaped the monarchy and the landscape.
It was first climbed in 1955; the climbers stopped just short of the summit out of respect.

data.claim: Organic Sikkim grows all its own food
data.why: The organic rule covers farm inputs; the state still buys much of its food from the plains.

data.claim: Hope Cooke was a CIA agent
data.why: A rumour repeated in India in the 1970s; no evidence has been published.
It freezes over most of the winter; the legend is that one blessed part stays open.
They came to Sikkim from Tibet and Nepal's Newar traders, though dumplings are a wider Asian family.
97.55% voted yes, on a turnout of about 63%, and critics still question how it was run.

sections.title: Recap
sections.intro_md:
Sikkim is India's least populous state and its second smallest, a 7,096 square km slope from the 280 m Teesta valley to the 8,586 m summit of Kangchenjunga, which its people treat as a god. It was a Buddhist kingdom from 1642 to 1975, ruled by the Namgyal Chogyals from Yuksom, Rabdentse, Tumlong and Gangtok, squeezed by Bhutan, Nepal, Britain and finally India.

Remember the people: the Lepcha first, the Bhutia kings, the Nepali majority; Hope Cooke, Kazi Lhendup Dorjee, Pawan Chamling, Bhaichung Bhutia. Remember the numbers: 97.55% in 1975, 12 official languages, 1.1 children per woman, about 75,000 organic hectares. And remember the warning of October 2023: a lake that grew for 50 years and emptied in a night.

side_dish.title: How a glacial lake becomes a flood
side_dish.body_md:
A glacial lake forms when a glacier retreats and meltwater pools behind the heap of rock and ice it left behind, called a moraine. That dam was never built to hold water. It is loose rubble, often cemented by ice or permafrost.

As the climate warms, three things happen at once. Glaciers melt faster, so the lake grows. The permafrost holding the moraine together thaws, so the dam weakens. And the slopes above the lake, also thawing, become more likely to collapse. When ice or rock falls into the lake, it sets off a wave that can overtop or cut through the dam. Then the whole lake empties down the valley in hours. Scientists call this a glacial lake outburst flood, or GLOF.

South Lhonak in North Sikkim is the textbook case. Satellite images show it growing from about 0.15 square km in 1975 to about 1.7 square km by 2023. A 2021 study named it among the most dangerous lakes in the Himalaya and said an avalanche was the likeliest trigger. On the night of 3 to 4 October 2023, that is roughly what happened.

The Himalaya has thousands of glacial lakes, and Indian agencies now track the ones judged high risk, several of them in Sikkim. Early-warning sensors, siphoning water to lower lakes, and not putting dams and towns right in the flood path are the main defences.

offline_task.title: Make Sikkim-style momos with a Dalle-style chutney
offline_task.body_md:
About an hour. Makes 20 to 24.

**Dough:** 2 cups maida, a pinch of salt, water to make a soft, smooth dough. Rest it covered for 20 minutes.

**Filling:** finely chop 2 cups of cabbage, 1 carrot, 1 onion, a handful of spring onion and coriander. Add 1 tsp grated ginger, 4 cloves garlic, salt and 1 tbsp oil. Squeeze out extra water. (For a Sikkim touch, crumble in a little paneer as a stand-in for soft chhurpi.)

**Shape:** roll small balls of dough into thin 8 cm circles, thinner at the edges. Put a spoon of filling in the middle and pleat the edge closed, either round like a purse or half-moon.

**Steam:** oil a steamer plate, leave gaps, steam 10 to 12 minutes until the dough is glossy.

**Chutney:** char 2 tomatoes, blend with 4 cloves garlic, salt and dried red chillies to taste. Sikkim uses the round Dalle chilli, among the hottest grown in India; use 1 or 2 if you find it.

While they steam, read the Kangchenjunga and Hope Cooke spotlights again and see how many facts you can still remember without looking.

best_facts.fact: The first climbers of Kangchenjunga, in 1955, stopped a few metres below the summit on purpose, keeping a promise to the Chogyal of Sikkim that the sacred top would not be trodden.
best_facts.why_surprising: Mountaineers almost never leave a summit unclimbed by choice.

best_facts.fact: Sikkim's last queen was Hope Cooke, a student from San Francisco who married the crown prince in 1963 and later became a historian of New York City.
best_facts.why_surprising: An American queen of a Himalayan Buddhist kingdom, in living memory.

best_facts.fact: Sikkim's fertility rate in 2019 to 2020 was 1.1 children per woman, the lowest in India and lower than many European countries; the state now pays government employees extra increments for a second or third child.
best_facts.why_surprising: India is usually discussed as a country with too many births, not too few.

best_facts.fact: In the 14 April 1975 referendum, 97.55% voted to abolish Sikkim's 333-year-old monarchy, and five weeks later it was India's 22nd state.
best_facts.why_surprising: A kingdom became a state in under six weeks.

best_facts.fact: Pawan Kumar Chamling ran Sikkim for about 24 and a half years, the longest any chief minister has served in India, then lost both seats he contested in 2024.
best_facts.why_surprising: The record holder lost personally, twice in one day.

best_facts.fact: Hard chhurpi, a Himalayan cheese, is so hard you hold a cube in your mouth for half an hour to five hours before it softens; Nepal now exports it as dog chews.
best_facts.why_surprising: A cheese that takes hours to eat.

best_facts.fact: A British botanist collecting rhododendrons, Joseph Hooker, was seized in Sikkim in 1849; Britain's response cost Sikkim land and, within 12 years, its independence in all but name.
best_facts.why_surprising: A plant-hunting trip changed a kingdom's borders.

best_facts.fact: The red panda was called a panda about 45 years before the giant panda was, and it is not closely related to it.
best_facts.why_surprising: The famous panda borrowed its name from the obscure one.

best_facts.fact: Every year lamas at Tashiding open a sealed vase of water and read Sikkim's coming year from its level: full means plenty, low means famine.
best_facts.why_surprising: A state-wide forecast from one pot of water.

best_facts.fact: In 2016 Sikkim became India's first fully organic state, banning chemical pesticides on about 75,000 hectares, and won a UN-backed Future Policy Gold Award in 2018.
best_facts.why_surprising: A whole state, not a farm, went organic.

best_facts.fact: Khangchendzonga National Park, listed in 2016, is India's only World Heritage Site listed equally for nature and culture: the culture is the belief that it is a hidden sacred land.
best_facts.why_surprising: Faith counted as heritage alongside snow leopards.

best_facts.fact: South Lhonak Lake grew more than tenfold between 1975 and 2023, then burst in one night, sweeping away a 1,200 MW dam and 31 bridges.
best_facts.why_surprising: Climate change turned a remote lake into the deadliest event in modern Sikkim.

best_facts.fact: Soldiers believe Sepoy Harbhajan Singh, who died near Nathu La in 1968, still guards the border; each year his belongings are sent home by train with a seat booked for him.
best_facts.why_surprising: A ghost with a train reservation.

best_facts.fact: Danny Denzongpa was born in Yuksom, the village where Sikkim's first king was crowned; his classmate Jaya Bhaduri gave him the name Danny, and he founded the north-east's biggest brewery.
best_facts.why_surprising: Bollywood's great villain is also a beer baron from a royal village.

best_facts.fact: The villages of Lachung and Lachen run themselves through a dzumsa, a household council with an elected headman called the pipon, which the state treats as their panchayat.
best_facts.why_surprising: India still has villages with their own pre-democratic parliaments.

best_facts.fact: Sikkim has 12 official languages for about six lakh people.
best_facts.why_surprising: More official languages per head than any other state.
